newsitem.title: INDIA: India faces prospect of turning cement importer.
newsitem.headline: India faces prospect of turning cement importer.

text.p: India runs the risk of turning into a cement importer from a leading exporter due to a recent railway freight hike that will steeply increase input costs, manufacturers and analysts said on Thursday.

"The railway freight hike will burden the industry with an additional (cost of) 7.0 billion rupees ($196 million) which the industry is in no position to absorb," said R. Partha Sarathy, secretary-general of India's cement manufacturers' association.
"The excessive taxes and levies will push up cement prices and erode the competence of the cement industry in the global market."
India on Wednesday announced a 12 percent increase in freight rates for most commodities, including cement, in the annual railway budget for 1997/98 (April-March).
"From being a foreign exchange earner, we face the prospect of turning into net importers," Partha Sarathy told a conference on the cement industry.

In 1995/96, India exported 2.4 million tonnes of cement. The country is the world's fourth largest cement producer and industry estimates say it will be the second largest producer after China by the year 2002.
India produced some 69 million tonnes of cement in 1995/96, or almost five percent of world's total cement output.
A 50-kg (110-lb) bag of cement will cost 4.50 rupees more after the rail freight increase, industry observers said. Nearly half of India's cement is moved by rail.
"Presently the cement industry is reeling under a depression and there is no way it can absorb the extra cost," Partha Sarathy said.
Analysts expect domestic cement demand to grow by 8.0 percent in 1996/97 against 11 percent in the previous year.
Cement makers said the government must announce tax cuts for the sector in the 1997/98 budget, due on Friday.
But Partha Sarathy said the sector feared the budget would replace the existing 350 rupee per tonne excise duty on cement with an ad valorem tax.
The cement industry is one of the biggest contributors to government revenues, paying about 18 billion rupees ($502 million) a year in direct and indirect taxes.
"Why kill the goose that lays the golden egg?" said one producer at the conference. ($1=35.88)
